class.ijn_ca_aoba.history: Aoba and Kinugasa were improved Furutakas with twin turrets. Both fought at Savo; at Cape Esperance in October 1942 Aoba was ambushed by radar-directed US cruisers and badly damaged, Kinugasa was sunk at Guadalcanal in November.
class.ijn_ca_furutaka.history: Japan's first generation of heavy cruisers, small but well armed. Kako was torpedoed by the submarine S-44 on 10 August 1942 while returning from Savo; Furutaka was sunk at Cape Esperance two months later.
class.ijn_ca_takao.history: The Takao class combined ten 20 cm guns with a towering bridge that housed the most elaborate fire-control and command spaces of any cruiser of her time. Chokai was Mikawa's flagship at Savo Island and was hit several times by Quincy's last salvoes.
class.ijn_ca_takao.tactics: Heavy gun and torpedo armament, excellent night optics. Keep the range short at night where its torpedoes and trained lookouts dominate.
class.ijn_cl_tenryu.history: Small light cruisers of 1919, designed as destroyer flotilla leaders. Old and lightly armed, they were still useful in night actions thanks to their torpedoes.
class.ijn_cl_yubari.history: An experimental design that packed a full light cruiser armament onto a 3,000-ton hull. Yubari fought at Savo Island at the end of Mikawa's column.
class.ijn_dd_fubuki.history: The 'Special Type' destroyers of 1928 shocked other navies with six 12.7 cm guns in enclosed mounts and nine 61 cm torpedo tubes with reloads. Ayanami fought alone against two US battleships off Savo in November 1942.
class.ijn_dd_kagero.history: The backbone of the 'Tokyo Express' supply runs to Guadalcanal. At Tassafaronga on 30 November 1942 Kagero-class destroyers turned a surprise attack by a superior US cruiser force into a Japanese victory with a mass torpedo launch.
class.ijn_dd_kagero.tactics: Fire torpedoes first, guns second. Reload at sea and attack again. Turn away immediately after launching.
class.ijn_dd_kamikaze.history: Destroyers of the early 1920s. Yunagi accompanied Mikawa to Savo Island and covered the withdrawal.
class.ijn_dd_shiratsuyu.history: The first Japanese destroyers with quadruple torpedo mounts. Yudachi caused havoc in the first naval battle of Guadalcanal; Shigure became famous as a lucky ship.
class.ijn_dd_yugumo.history: Improved Kageros with higher-angle guns. Takanami was lost at Tassafaronga after drawing the fire of the entire US force.
class.ran_ca_kent.history: A British 'County' class treaty cruiser with high freeboard and long range, built for imperial trade protection rather than close combat. HMAS Canberra was hit by more than twenty shells and two torpedoes in the first minutes at Savo Island and had to be scuttled.
class.usn_ap_transport.history: Converted liners and freighters that carried the Marines to Guadalcanal. Their protection was the reason the cruisers stood guard around Savo Island.
class.usn_ca_new_orleans.history: The last US 'treaty' heavy cruisers, with better armour than their predecessors. Astoria, Quincy and Vincennes were all sunk at Savo Island - surprised, illuminated by searchlights and shot to pieces before they could reply effectively.
class.usn_ca_new_orleans.tactics: Strong gun platform. Do not let the enemy close at night unseen: keep crews at battle stations near enemy waters and use radar early.
class.usn_ca_northampton.history: Northampton-class cruisers carried nine 8-inch guns in three triple turrets. USS Chicago lost her bow to a torpedo at Savo and failed to warn the northern group; Northampton herself was sunk by Long Lance torpedoes at Tassafaronga.
class.usn_ca_pensacola.history: The first US treaty cruisers, with ten 8-inch guns but thin armour. Salt Lake City fought at Cape Esperance; Pensacola survived a Long Lance hit at Tassafaronga.
class.usn_cl_brooklyn.history: Fifteen rapid-firing 6-inch guns gave the Brooklyns a tremendous volume of fire at short and medium range. Boise was badly hit at Cape Esperance after illuminating a target with her searchlight.
class.usn_cl_brooklyn.tactics: Volume of fire, not penetration: overwhelm cruisers and destroyers at 8-12 km. Avoid searchlights - they mark you for every enemy gun.
class.usn_cl_st_louis.history: A refined Brooklyn with 5-inch/38 dual-purpose guns. USS Helena's SG surface radar gave the first warning at Cape Esperance - the turning point of radar in night actions.
class.usn_dd_bagley.history: Destroyers with sixteen torpedo tubes. Blue and Ralph Talbot were the radar pickets that failed to detect Mikawa at Savo; Bagley and Patterson screened the southern group.
class.usn_dd_benson.history: Benson/Gleaves-class destroyers formed many of the screens in the Solomons. Laffey fought at point-blank range against the battleship Hiei in November 1942.
class.usn_dd_fletcher.history: The definitive US destroyer of the war: five 5-inch/38 guns, ten torpedo tubes and good radar. Fletcher herself fought at Guadalcanal and Tassafaronga.
class.usn_dd_mahan.history: Mid-1930s destroyers with twelve torpedo tubes. Cushing led the US column into the first naval battle of Guadalcanal.

credits.history_text: Ship and weapon data use commonly published figures, rounded and simplified for play. Further reading: NavWeaps (navweaps.com), Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1922-1946, S. E. Morison 'History of United States Naval Operations in World War II' vol. V, R. Lundgren 'The World Wonder'd', J. D. Hornfischer 'Neptune's Inferno'.

scenario.cape_esperance.briefing: Night of 11/12 October 1942, off Cape Esperance, the north-western tip of Guadalcanal. To cover a convoy bringing Army reinforcements to the Marines, Rear Admiral Norman Scott's Task Group 64.2 - the heavy cruisers San Francisco and Salt Lake City, the light cruisers Boise and Helena and five destroyers - waits between Savo Island and the cape. Rear Admiral Aritomo Gotō is coming down 'the Slot' with the heavy cruisers Aoba, Furutaka and Kinugasa and two destroyers to shell Henderson Field, while a separate Japanese group lands troops and artillery further along the coast. The moon has set, the sky is overcast, the sea calm.
scenario.cape_esperance.history: Helena's SG radar found Gotō's force at about 23:25, but the report reached Scott only as his column was countermarching, and the van destroyers ended up between the two forces. Even so the Americans crossed the Japanese 'T'. At 23:46 Helena opened fire without waiting for orders and the others followed. Gotō, convinced he was being fired on by friendly ships, turned away too late and was mortally wounded on Aoba's bridge. Furutaka and the destroyer Fubuki were sunk and Aoba badly damaged. The Americans lost Duncan, caught between both lines; Farenholt was hit by friendly shells, and Boise survived a magazine fire only because the sea flooding in through a shell hole put it out. It was the US Navy's first victory in a night surface action - yet the Japanese reinforcements were landed all the same.
scenario.cape_esperance.intel_allies: Search aircraft reported Japanese cruisers and destroyers coming down the Slot at high speed this afternoon. Expect them off Savo Island around midnight. Against cruisers the SG radar reaches about 25 km.
scenario.cape_esperance.intel_axis: Air reconnaissance found only American cruisers and destroyers far to the south of Guadalcanal. Our own reinforcement group is unloading off the coast tonight - ships sighted near Savo may well be friendly.
scenario.cape_esperance.orders_allies: Intercept the Japanese force west of Savo Island before it can shell Henderson Field. Your crews have trained for exactly this night action and are at battle stations. Helena and Boise carry the new SG search radar - use it, but keep the column together: identification at night is uncertain and your own destroyers steam ahead of the cruisers.
scenario.cape_esperance.orders_axis: Take the bombardment group past Savo Island, shell Henderson Field and withdraw to the north-west before dawn. No American surface ships are expected - they have not contested these waters at night since August. Your crews are at cruising stations, the guns trained fore and aft.
scenario.cape_esperance.title: Battle of Cape Esperance
scenario.savo_island.briefing: Night of 8/9 August 1942, Ironbottom Sound off Guadalcanal. Two days ago US Marines landed on Guadalcanal and Tulagi; the transports are still unloading off Lunga Point. Vice Admiral Gunichi Mikawa has raced down from Rabaul with five heavy cruisers, two light cruisers and a destroyer. The Allied screen is split around Savo Island: a southern group (HMAS Canberra, USS Chicago and two destroyers), a northern group (Vincennes, Quincy, Astoria and two destroyers) and two radar pickets west of the island. The night is dark and overcast, rain squalls drift over the sound, the moon has set.
scenario.savo_island.history: Historically Mikawa's column slipped past the picket destroyers unseen. Floatplanes dropped flares over the southern group; within minutes Canberra was wrecked by gunfire and Chicago lost her bow to a torpedo, without warning the northern group. Mikawa swept around Savo and destroyed Vincennes, Quincy and Astoria in close-range night action. More than a thousand Allied sailors died. Fearing air attack at dawn, Mikawa withdrew without attacking the transports; on the way home Kako was sunk by the submarine S-44. It remains one of the heaviest defeats ever suffered by the US Navy.
scenario.savo_island.intel_allies: A sighting by an Australian Hudson on 8 August reported 'three cruisers, three destroyers and two seaplane tenders' heading south-east - read as a force setting up a seaplane base. The report arrived hours late. No surface attack is expected tonight.
scenario.savo_island.intel_axis: Reconnaissance on 7 August reported several cruisers and destroyers covering the landing. Expect patrol lines on both sides of Savo Island; destroyers with radar may be posted to the west.
scenario.savo_island.orders_allies: Guard both entrances to the anchorage around Savo Island and stop any surface force before it reaches the transports. Your crews have been at action stations for two days and are now in Condition II - raising the alarm will cost precious minutes. Radar (SC on the destroyers) is unreliable close to land.
scenario.savo_island.orders_axis: Pass Savo Island undetected, destroy the Allied cruisers in a night action and, if possible, strike the transports off Lunga Point. Break off in time: by daylight you must be out of range of American carrier aircraft. Japanese night training, Type 93 torpedoes and surprise are your weapons.
scenario.savo_island.title: Battle of Savo Island
scenario.tassafaronga.briefing: Night of 30 November 1942, off Tassafaronga Point on the north coast of Guadalcanal. Rear Admiral Raizō Tanaka's Destroyer Squadron 2 - eight destroyers - is running the 'Tokyo Express': six of them carry drums of food and supplies lashed on deck, to be dropped off the coast and hauled ashore by the starving garrison. To make room, the drum ships left their reload torpedoes behind. Rear Admiral Carleton Wright, in command of Task Force 67 for only two days, is coming in through Lengo Channel with four heavy cruisers, a light cruiser and six destroyers to stop them. The night is very dark and the sea calm; against the jungle-covered shore the Japanese ships are almost invisible.
scenario.tassafaronga.history: American radar picked up the Japanese at about 23:06, but Wright hesitated before releasing his destroyers' torpedoes; when they were finally fired the range had opened and none hit. The cruisers' gunfire fell mostly on Takanami, the nearest Japanese ship, which was wrecked and sunk. Tanaka's other destroyers turned away and launched more than forty torpedoes without firing a gun. Minutes later Minneapolis, New Orleans, Pensacola and Northampton were hit: Minneapolis and New Orleans lost their bows, Pensacola burned for hours, and Northampton sank after midnight. One Japanese destroyer lost against one heavy cruiser sunk and three crippled - Tassafaronga became a textbook example of the torpedo tactics of the IJN, even though no supplies were landed that night.
scenario.tassafaronga.intel_allies: Coast watchers and radio intelligence predict a run of eight destroyers, possibly with transports, to Guadalcanal tonight. Expect them along the coast off Tassafaronga around 23:00.
scenario.tassafaronga.intel_axis: American cruisers and destroyers have been seen in the area during the last days; their position tonight is unknown. Expect to be opposed. None of our ships carries radar.
scenario.tassafaronga.orders_allies: Intercept the Tokyo Express off Tassafaronga and destroy it. The plan: the van destroyers attack first with radar-aimed torpedoes, then the cruisers open fire at about 11 km. Your SG radars see the enemy long before any lookout - the Japanese have no radar, but they have the most dangerous torpedoes afloat.
scenario.tassafaronga.orders_axis: Reach the drop point off Tassafaronga, release the supply drums and withdraw to the north-west. Avoid action if you can - but if enemy cruisers appear, your crews know what to do: turn away, launch the Type 93s unseen and let the torpedoes do the work.
scenario.tassafaronga.title: Battle of Tassafaronga

torpedo.ijn_type93.note: The 'Long Lance': a 61 cm oxygen-fuelled torpedo with enormous range and a heavy warhead. It leaves almost no wake - at night it arrives unseen. The Allies did not know of its performance in 1942 and kept mistaking torpedo hits for submarine attacks.
torpedo.usn_mk15.note: The standard US destroyer torpedo. In 1942 its Mark 6 exploder and depth control were unreliable: many hits failed to explode or the torpedoes ran too deep.
